cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the ground holds steady under it.
cells.ask: Offer one person something small today — a question, a hand — and take what comes back without sorting it first.
cells.core:
Something in you is open before anything has been poured in. That's not emptiness. It's the part before a feeling gets a name, and you're standing in it well — what you feel lands clean and you don't grip it or push it off. When someone brings you something, you can take it in and hand something back without either of you disappearing into the other.

That even exchange is what keeps the open part open. It doesn't stay by itself — it gets fed by contact, one clean back-and-forth at a time, and that back-and-forth is what tells you the evenness is real. So let someone offer you something today and stay there while they do it, without glancing at what you'll owe. Keep the accepting and the answering close together. The exchange is the thing doing the feeding.
cells.sheetLine: Something is open in you, and it isn't asking you to fill it.
cells.verb: standing open with nothing yet in your hands

cells.tense: You are already living past today, bracing against what hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Before answering anyone today, take one breath and name one thing you actually want from the conversation. Then answer from it.
cells.core:
You can feel what's coming before it gets here. A conversation gets set up and you've already written the ending, already shaped yourself to someone else's likely reaction. Your feeling is open early and you're filling it ahead of time. Even your sense of what's fair runs ahead — you're weighing what you'll owe and what you'll be owed before anything has actually happened.

The readiness is real; it just keeps jumping ahead of the room. What's underneath it — the part that can know something without needing to finish it — is still there. It doesn't need more foresight. It needs you where the exchange is actually happening, and there's a want in you that hasn't been said out loud. Name it before you speak. See whether the fairness lands differently once it's your actual position and not your forecast.

cells.tense: You stand a step back from a door that is already behind you.
cells.ask: Say yes to one small thing without checking it first — a plan, an offer, a walk — and go. Let the yes itself count.
cells.core:
The open part went quiet. Nobody is holding anything shut; the receiving just stopped, and you stand a step back from it. Other people's feeling doesn't land on you the way it used to, and you call that being even-keeled. The fairness you run is careful and correct. It's the entrance that's closed, not the arithmetic.

What's still yours is the first moment of anything — the raw part before a feeling gets a name. That's what's gone thin, not your judgment. It doesn't come back by trying to feel more; pushing on a hollowed-out stretch just locks it harder. It comes back when one small thing is allowed in, fresh, with no plan made for it. Let an invitation arrive without checking whether it's sensible. The entrance opens from the side of the new, not the side of the fair.
cells.sheetLine: Your fairness is precise. The entering has gone quiet.

cells.tense: You are already balancing it all, and you talk about it as if it were doing the balancing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you gave that nobody asked for and one thing you were given and didn't count. Say both out loud, once.
cells.core:
You're already feeling this — the mood of a room, what a person needs before they ask, the exact moment things go uneven. And you're already adjusting for it. What you call being polite or paying your share is you, reading a situation and moving to set it right. The skill runs all day. You report it as though it happened on its own.

The openness you have isn't the loud kind that makes a fuss about itself. It works quietly and gets taken for granted, often by you. But the reading that keeps things even can also keep the uncounted parts out of sight — the gift nobody noticed, the effort that went on no ledger. Saying that plain isn't scorekeeping. It just hands the receiving back to the one who has been doing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one doing the balancing. Say so, once.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person is being unfair or that fairness is something they've stopped doing — Equity is where the capacity landed, so my cells stay off 'you've been unjust to people' and keep to how readiness is met or missed. A reader could reasonably say their fairness is fine and it's the readiness that's been wrong, which is why every cell keeps the fairness talk at the level of a moment they could recognise. The asks still work if my read is wrong: each one is something they can do anyway, on any day, and none of them promises a result. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything that would let me sound wise about their history — 'you learned early that receiving ends badly' — so none of it is here.
